extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of moral philosophy; readers interested in foundations of ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Extract and apply criteria for what constitutes a sound foundation for Ethics (theory of morality), focusing on empirical adequacy, motives, conscience, and the relation of moral rules to social institutions. Useful for assessing ethical theories and their explanatory power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical foundation required
rubrics_metrics.description: There remains no way of discovering the basis of Ethics except the empirical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The foundation of Ethics must be reached by following the empirical path: search for actions with genuine moral worth and investigate their real origin; rely on experience which 'daily and hourly delivers its silent testimony' rather than on a priori constructions or absolute legislation for all rational beings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for genuine moral worth
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethics must point to actions to which we are obliged to ascribe 'genuine moral worth': voluntary justice, pure loving-kindness, and true nobleness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A satisfactory foundation must identify such actions as given phenomena and explain the peculiar motives and susceptibilities that produce them, distinguishing them from actions motivated by external or egoistic incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and intuitive accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The foundation must be 'something that requires but little reflection, and still less abstraction and complicated synthesis; something that, independent of the training of the understanding, speaks to every one, even to the rudest.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid elaborate artificial subtlety, stilted maxims, and needle-point distinctions; a real moral foundation should present principles that naturally incline people to act justly and kindly in ordinary life, not only appeal to trained intellects in lecture-rooms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject theological/a priori imperative as sole basis
rubrics_metrics.description: The conception of 'ought' (the imperative form of Ethics) is valid only in theological morals, outside of which it loses all sense and meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foundations that rest on a priori categorical imperatives or theological presuppositions (e.g., Kantian absolute 'Ought' or divine-legislation-style accounts) are inadmissible as general ethical foundations for human life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain motives and susceptibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The ultimate basis of morality consists of the motives, together with a responsive susceptibility for them, which lead men to actions distinct from others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethical theory must trace moral conduct to specific motives and the capacity to respond to them; it must offer an account of how these motives operate and produce disinterested or noble actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start from egoism as fundamental incentive
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief and fundamental incentive in man, as in animals, is Egoism — the urgent impulse to exist, and exist under the best circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any account of moral action must first turn to Egoism as the general explanatory principle and then show how genuine moral action arises despite, or through modification of, this basic impulse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate true and false conscience
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a conscientia spuria (false conscience) often confounded with the true; regret or anxiety for wrongdoing can be merely fear of consequences, habit, vanity, superstition, or social pressure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foundations must critically assess conscience, distinguishing elements due to external sanctions or internalized social codes from a natural, genuine moral sense; examples include religiously inculcated scruples or codes of 'honour' that are not moral in the substantive sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for role of social/legal restraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Much correct conduct depends on two external necessities: legal ordinance (state enforcement) and the recognised need of possessing civil honour (a good name) enforced by public opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proper foundation must explain how law, public opinion, and the desire for reputation function as 'custodians' of correct conduct, and must separate outward conformity enforced by these institutions from inward moral motivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain rare instances of disinterested virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: There are isolated, indisputable cases where, even with discovery and reward excluded, people return lost goods or keep deposits — 'there are in truth really honest people.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethical foundations must accommodate and explain such exceptional cases of disinterested behaviour (four-leaved-clover phenomenon) rather than dismissing them as illusion or purely self-interested calculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical testability via observing behavior when restraints removed
rubrics_metrics.description: To discover what human beings are morally, we must study anarchist records and criminal proceedings; if the state's muzzle were cast off, the spectacle would reveal true moral character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theories should be verifiable by empirical observation of conduct in situations where legal and reputational constraints are weakened; a foundation gains credibility if it explains behavior under such conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical theory must motivate real action
rubrics_metrics.description: Artificial associations and lecture-room niceties cannot contain the true incentive to justice and loving-kindness; the foundation must produce the impulse to act justly and to do good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An adequate foundation is one that yields practical moral incentives felt in ordinary life; it must be more than formal rules or abstractions that fail to move people to virtuous action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish natural right from positive right
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural right attaches to property gained by one's own exertion; positive right (civil/title) often stands at a distance from its natural source and depends on institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foundations should clarify how ethical motives relate to natural rights (original ownership) versus positive legal titles, and explain why positive-right holdings often lack direct moral justification without institutional backing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid construing moral explanations as merely scholastic or pedantic
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophic systems of fine distinctions and subtle formulae may be 'adapted for the lecture-room' but cannot be the cause of moral impulse; Kantian pedantry and Fichtean magnifications are cited as examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating ethical foundations, be wary of theories that prioritize argumentative cleverness, bombast, or formal consistency at the cost of explanatory power for real moral motivation and conduct.
